title: A beautiful thing (Matthew 26:1–16)
hookLine: a whole jar of perfume poured out, a room full of objections, and thirty pieces of silver
tomorrow: "one of you shall betray me." what would you ask first?

lines: MONEY ON SOMETHING THAT WON'T LAST.
TO WHAT PURPOSE IS THIS WASTE?
cards: Somebody spends real money on something that won't last: a huge bouquet, a fancy dinner, a concert ticket for a friend. And somebody else says it out loud: you could have done something useful with that.
In Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, a woman comes in with an alabaster box of very precious ointment and pours it on Jesus' head. Matthew gives her no lines.
The disciples talk instead, and they're indignant: "To what purpose is this waste?" It could have been sold, they say, and given to the poor.

teach.h: SHE HATH WROUGHT A GOOD WORK.
teach.b: It's a fair point, on paper. But Matthew has just turned a page: Jesus has finished all these sayings, the Passover is two days off, and he has told them where this is going. So he doesn't take the point.
"Why trouble ye the woman? for she hath wrought a good work upon me." The King James says a good work; some newer translations say a beautiful thing, which gives the day its title.

teach.h: SHE DID IT FOR MY BURIAL.
teach.b: Then he names what nobody saw: "she did it for my burial."

teach.h: TOLD FOR A MEMORIAL OF HER.
teach.b: And a promise: "Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her."
Here's one to tell a friend: Matthew keeps the promise and loses the name. What she did is told; who she was, he never says. Then the very next scene.
Judas goes to the chief priests and asks, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?"
Thirty pieces of silver. Matthew sets them side by side: one pours out something precious and asks for nothing; one sells him and asks what he can get.

how: Some churches read Matthew 26 in Holy Week, the week before Easter, and remember this unnamed woman as the one who anointed Jesus before his burial.

o: the anointing oil kept in the Temple for kings
a costly gift poured out for Jesus, which he defends
a perfume merchant Jesus praises for honest work

games.q: a beautiful thing — tap the pairs.
p: to what purpose is this waste?
she did it for my burial

s: in Matthew, the woman pours the ointment on Jesus' feet
in Matthew it's his head (26:7). other Gospels tell anointing stories with differences.
Matthew tells us the woman's name
he doesn't. what she did is told for a memorial of her; her name isn't kept.
the disciples said the ointment could have been sold for the poor
"for this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor."

games.q: you ran the whole canned-food drive. the school newsletter thanks someone else by name. by Matthew 26, what lasts?
o: what you did: her name is lost and her gift is still told.
only the name: a memorial needs someone to credit.
nothing: work nobody credits is work wasted.
games.why: Jesus promises that what this woman hath done will be told for a memorial of her, and Matthew never gives her name. the deed outlasts the credit.

practice: Find something with a scent near you: soap on your hands, coffee, an orange peel, a candle, a sweater that smells like someone. Breathe it in slowly, the way that room in Bethany must have filled.
While it lingers, bring to mind one person you'd love to spend something beautiful on, with no thought of whether it's useful. The scent doesn't have to be useful either; let it stay.

wordCard.voice: A beautiful thing. In the King James, a good work: precious ointment poured on Jesus' head, told wherever the gospel goes.

orig.note: Greek: the good work Jesus names in Matthew 26:10; some translations say a beautiful thing.

carryVoice: Your line: wherever this gospel is preached. Her name is lost, and her gift is still told. Week done.
